script.problem: It reuses a line from the Prep cards word for word.

terra.problem: The cookie-box joke does not match the action of the family relocating, and it is unclear why moving a box would require opening it.
The explanation is flat, and the final sentence merely says the passage names the women before continuing.
Naomi expresses a wish to the women, but the explanation turns it into a request that the LORD act. The voice rules call for keeping her statement as a 'May the LORD' wish.
The explanation describes Naomi as asking that the LORD act rather than expressing her wish to the women.
Saying Ruth will be buried where Naomi is buried adds a detail the verse does not give. Ruth says she will die where Naomi dies and be buried there.
The explanation implies Naomi will be buried where she dies. Ruth says she herself will die and be buried where Naomi dies, but does not state where Naomi will be buried.
The cookie joke does not match Naomi stopping her attempts to persuade Ruth. It shifts to Papa's difficulty resisting a cookie instead.
Naomi asks to be called Mara instead of Naomi, not instead of Leah.

explanations.explanation: Moab is the destination, friend. The man takes his wife and two sons from Bethlehem in Judah to live there during the famine (Ruth 1:1). I need three attempts just to move a cookie box without opening it.

Egypt isn't the destination named here, baker. This family leaves Bethlehem in Judah and goes to live in Moab (Ruth 1:1). Keep those two places together: Bethlehem is where they leave, and Moab is where they settle (Ruth 1:1-2).
The place we're looking for is Moab. Ruth 1:1 names it as the land where the family goes to live. Bethlehem in Judah is their starting point, not their destination (Ruth 1:1).
Ruth is the other woman named, friend. She and Orpah are the Moabite women who marry Naomi's sons (Ruth 1:4). The passage gives both their names before telling us what happens next (Ruth 1:4-5).
The name here is Ruth, baker. Naomi's sons marry two Moabite women named Orpah and Ruth (Ruth 1:4). Rachel isn't named as either wife in this passage (Ruth 1:4).
Ruth is the name that belongs beside Orpah here. Those are the two women Naomi's sons marry in Moab (Ruth 1:4). Keep that pair together as we follow the family, friend.

Both sons, Mahlon and Chilion, die after the family has lived in Moab about ten years (Ruth 1:4-5). Naomi has now lost her husband and both sons (Ruth 1:3-5). I think this is a moment to slow down, friend.

explanations.answer: Her house in Moab burns down
explanations.explanation: The passage doesn't report a house fire. It tells us that both of Naomi's sons die (Ruth 1:5). Her husband has already died too, so she is left without her husband and her two sons (Ruth 1:3-5).

explanations.answer: She falls sick and loses her sight
explanations.explanation: An illness or loss of sight isn't reported here. What happens is that Mahlon and Chilion, Naomi's two sons, both die (Ruth 1:5). Naomi is left without them and without her husband (Ruth 1:5).
Food is the news that reaches Naomi. She hears in Moab that the LORD has provided it for His people (Ruth 1:6). After hearing that, she and her daughters-in-law prepare to leave Moab (Ruth 1:6).

This report isn't about a king, friend. Naomi hears that the LORD has attended to His people by providing food (Ruth 1:6). The chapter began with a famine, so notice the change in that news (Ruth 1:1, 6).
The news here concerns food, not a victory. Naomi hears that the LORD has provided food for His people (Ruth 1:6). She and her daughters-in-law then get ready to leave Moab (Ruth 1:6).

explanations.answer: Go back to their mothers' homes
explanations.explanation: Naomi tells each woman to return to her mother's home (Ruth 1:8). Both daughters-in-law had started along the road with her (Ruth 1:7). Now she is urging them to turn back rather than continue with her (Ruth 1:8).

explanations.answer: Walk faster to beat the dark
explanations.explanation: Naomi isn't giving them a deadline for the journey. She tells each of them to go back to her mother's home (Ruth 1:8). This is about turning back, not picking up the pace, friend.

explanations.answer: Stay close to her the whole way
explanations.explanation: Both women are already traveling with Naomi when she speaks (Ruth 1:7-8). But she tells them to return to their mothers' homes, not to stay beside her (Ruth 1:8). The direction of her request matters here, baker.

Naomi does speak of each woman finding rest in a new husband's home (Ruth 1:9). She asks that the LORD enable this for each of them (Ruth 1:9). Notice, friend, that she speaks of rest, not merely a wedding (Ruth 1:9).

Those words about a new husband really are part of Naomi's send-off. She asks that the LORD enable each woman to find rest in that husband's home (Ruth 1:9). Then she kisses them, and they weep aloud (Ruth 1:9).

explanations.answer: We will return with you to your people
explanations.explanation: At this point, both women say they will return with Naomi to her people (Ruth 1:10). Naomi has told them to go home, but their answer is that they will accompany her (Ruth 1:8-10). Keep an eye on who is speaking here, friend: this is still both daughters-in-law.

explanations.answer: We will stay in Moab and wait for you
explanations.explanation: Their answer is about going with Naomi, not waiting for her. Both women say they will return with her to her people (Ruth 1:10). They haven't agreed to turn back at this point (Ruth 1:10).

explanations.answer: We will come visit you in Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: They don't offer a later visit here. They say they will return with Naomi to her people (Ruth 1:10). Their reply is a commitment to accompany her, not a promise to stop by sometime (Ruth 1:10).

explanations.answer: Would you wait for them to grow up
explanations.explanation: Naomi asks whether they would wait for those sons to grow up (Ruth 1:13). She is considering an imagined situation in which she had a husband that night and bore sons (Ruth 1:12). She also asks whether they would refrain from having husbands while they waited (Ruth 1:13).

explanations.answer: Would you raise them as your own
explanations.explanation: Naomi isn't asking the women to raise children for her. She asks whether they would wait for imagined sons to grow up and refrain from having husbands (Ruth 1:12-13). The question is about waiting for husbands, not becoming mothers to those sons (Ruth 1:11-13).

explanations.answer: Would you go ahead to Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: This question isn't about traveling ahead, friend. Naomi asks whether they would wait for sons to grow up if she were to bear them (Ruth 1:12-13). She also asks whether they would refrain from having husbands during that wait (Ruth 1:13).

explanations.answer: The LORD's hand has turned against her
explanations.explanation: That is the reason Naomi gives for her bitterness (Ruth 1:13). She says that the hand of the LORD has gone out against her (Ruth 1:13). We're hearing Naomi's own account of her suffering here, friend.

explanations.answer: The people of Judah have turned against her
explanations.explanation: Naomi doesn't accuse the people of Judah in this statement. She says her situation is more bitter because the LORD's hand has gone out against her (Ruth 1:13). Keep her words attached to her, friend: this is what Naomi says about her suffering.

explanations.answer: The people of Moab have turned against her
explanations.explanation: Naomi doesn't name the people of Moab as the cause here. Her stated reason is that the hand of the LORD has gone out against her (Ruth 1:13). The verse gives us her words, not an account of the Moabites turning against her (Ruth 1:13).
Orpah does kiss Naomi goodbye (Ruth 1:14). Both daughters-in-law weep aloud again before Orpah's farewell (Ruth 1:14). Ruth, meanwhile, clings to Naomi (Ruth 1:14).

The goodbye kiss is Orpah's action in this verse (Ruth 1:14). Ruth is the one who clings to Naomi (Ruth 1:14). The passage places those two actions side by side, so keep each woman with her own action, friend.
Ruth doesn't go back with Orpah. Orpah kisses Naomi goodbye, but Ruth clings to her (Ruth 1:14). That difference matters as the conversation continues, friend.

Ruth stays with Naomi rather than returning with Orpah (Ruth 1:14). The verse says Orpah kisses Naomi goodbye while Ruth clings to her (Ruth 1:14). Two women have traveled beside Naomi, but they do not make the same choice here (Ruth 1:7, 14).

Naomi does tell Ruth, her daughter-in-law, to follow Orpah home (Ruth 1:15). She points out that Orpah has returned to her people and her gods (Ruth 1:15). Naomi is still urging Ruth to turn back at this point (Ruth 1:15).

Naomi really does urge Ruth to follow Orpah back home (Ruth 1:15). She says Orpah has gone back to her people and her gods (Ruth 1:15). This is another appeal for Ruth to leave, not an invitation to keep traveling together (Ruth 1:15).

explanations.answer: Naomi's God will be her God
explanations.explanation: Ruth promises that Naomi's God will be her God (Ruth 1:16). She also commits to Naomi's people and to living wherever Naomi lives (Ruth 1:16). Her answer reaches beyond simply sharing the road, friend.

explanations.answer: She will take care of Naomi's house
explanations.explanation: Taking care of a house isn't the promise Ruth names here. She says Naomi's people will be her people and Naomi's God will be her God (Ruth 1:16). Listen to how much of her life that commitment includes, baker.

explanations.answer: She will learn all the ways of Judah
explanations.explanation: Ruth doesn't make that particular promise in this verse. She commits herself to Naomi's people and to Naomi's God (Ruth 1:16). She also says she will go where Naomi goes and live where Naomi lives (Ruth 1:16).

Death is the word Ruth uses in this solemn promise (Ruth 1:17). She calls for the LORD to punish her severely if anything but death separates them (Ruth 1:17). She also says she will die and be buried where Naomi does (Ruth 1:17).

Ruth names death, not distance, as the separation in her oath (Ruth 1:17). She has already promised to go wherever Naomi goes and live wherever Naomi lives (Ruth 1:16). Now she speaks of dying and being buried where Naomi does (Ruth 1:17).

Marriage isn't the exception Ruth names. Her oath says that nothing but death is to separate her from Naomi (Ruth 1:17). She calls for severe punishment from the LORD if anything else separates them (Ruth 1:17).

explanations.answer: She stops trying to persuade her
explanations.explanation: Naomi stops trying to persuade Ruth when she sees Ruth is determined to go with her (Ruth 1:18). That is the reason the verse gives, friend. I sometimes tell myself I'll leave one cookie untouched, but I have yet to sound that convincing.

explanations.answer: She sends her back after Orpah
explanations.explanation: Naomi had urged Ruth to follow Orpah earlier (Ruth 1:15). But after seeing Ruth's determination, she stops trying to persuade her (Ruth 1:18). Notice the change between the earlier request and what Naomi does now.

explanations.answer: She tells her to wait in Moab
explanations.explanation: Naomi doesn't tell Ruth to wait behind in Moab here. She sees that Ruth is determined to accompany her and stops trying to persuade her (Ruth 1:18). The two then travel on to Bethlehem together (Ruth 1:19).

The women exclaim, “Can this be Naomi?” (Ruth 1:19). The whole town is stirred when Naomi and Ruth arrive (Ruth 1:19). You know how one message can wake up a silent group chat, and suddenly your phone needs a rest.

That isn't the question the women ask in this scene. Their recorded words are, “Can this be Naomi?” (Ruth 1:19). The passage reports the whole town being stirred because of Naomi and Ruth's arrival (Ruth 1:19).

The women's question names Naomi rather than asking about a stranger (Ruth 1:19). They exclaim, “Can this be Naomi?” (Ruth 1:19). Keep your attention on those words, friend, because Naomi's answer follows them (Ruth 1:20).
Mara is the name Naomi asks them to use (Ruth 1:20). She says the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with her (Ruth 1:20). I hear pain in that answer, friend.

The name Naomi requests is Mara, not Hannah (Ruth 1:20). She connects that request with her statement that the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with her (Ruth 1:20). We're listening to Naomi describe her own experience here.

Naomi asks to be called Mara rather than Leah (Ruth 1:20). Her explanation is that the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with her (Ruth 1:20). I think that makes this much more than a request to use a different name.
Naomi describes the order the other way around. She says she went away full and the LORD has brought her back empty (Ruth 1:21). Those are Naomi's words about her return, friend.
The statement reverses Naomi's words. She says she left full but the LORD brought her back empty (Ruth 1:21). She also says the Almighty has afflicted her (Ruth 1:21).
Barley is the harvest named, baker. Naomi and Ruth reach Bethlehem at the beginning of that harvest (Ruth 1:22). That's where this passage leaves them, but their story isn't finished.
The harvest here is barley, not wheat (Ruth 1:22). The verse places Naomi and Ruth's arrival at its beginning (Ruth 1:22). Hold on to that timing, friend, because the story is still unfolding.

Barley is the crop named at the close of this passage (Ruth 1:22). Naomi returns from Moab with Ruth as that harvest begins (Ruth 1:22). They've reached Bethlehem, but we haven't reached the end of their story.
